title: Classification of Optical Filters According to Their Algorithmic Complexity and Impact on Visual Acuity
content: Purpose: To classify optical filters with different filtering levels according to their algorithmic complexity and to evaluate their effects on visual acuity (VA). The Block Decomposition Method (BDM) was applied to classify optical filters based on their estimated algorithmic complexity. Methods: VA was measured in all participants. Optical filters were analyzed using conventional statistical methods together with the BDM to characterize their algorithmic complexity. Results: Selective absorption filters exhibited a progressive reduction in transmittance within the blue spectral region (380–500 nm), accompanied by a shift of the cutoff wavelength toward longer wavelengths and a reduction in effective bandwidth, while maintaining relatively stable overall visible transmittance. Shannon entropy analysis revealed a progressive increase in statistical diversity as filter treatment time increased. In contrast, the algorithmic complexity estimated using the BDM exhibited a non-linear behavior, reaching its highest values in filters treated for 1 and 2 minutes. VA analysis performed on 235 eyes showed that the algorithmic complexity of visual responses depended on the visual function evaluated. Resolution acuity exhibited a decreasing trend in the estimated algorithmic complexity of its computational representation, whereas alignment acuity showed an overall increase across filter conditions. Detection acuity displayed non-linear changes, while recognition acuity included the highest individual nBDM value among the visual functions evaluated. Conclusions: Algorithmic complexity provides a complementary approach to conventional statistical methods for the analysis of ophthalmic filters and visual responses. The results indicate that statistical diversity and estimated algorithmic complexity characterize distinct and complementary properties of the computational representations analyzed. Selective absorption filters were associated with changes in the computational organization of the transmittance spectra and with differences in the computational representations of visual responses. BDM provided information about algorithmic organization that was complementary to conventional descriptive statistics and Shannon entropy, supporting its potential use as an additional computational tool for the characterization of photoselective filters and their relationship with visual performance.
